metric_rationale: This is the empirical effect of the second high-validity cue when the Tallying score is tied. In this fixed design, the two d=0 pairs have feature 0 tied and feature 2 discriminating. Take The Best says feature 2 then breaks the tie, so the B-choice rate should be higher when feature 2 favors B than when feature 2 favors A; in expectation the contrast is (1 - epsilon) * (2 * sigmoid(beta) - 1), where sigmoid(beta) = 1 / (1 + exp(-beta)). Tallying gives feature 2 no special weight; with equal win counts both d=0 cells have choice probability 0.5 under softmax and lapse, so the signed contrast is zero. The per-subject variance is limited because each subject contributes 12 repetitions to each side of the contrast.

This metric is a within-subject first-discriminating-cue contrast: P(choose A | the highest-validity cue that differs favors A) minus P(choose A | it favors B). In this design every trial is exactly tally-balanced, so Tallying predicts P(A)=0.5 in both trial classes and the contrast is 0. Take The Best predicts choices follow the first discriminating cue in validity order, so the A-favoring class should be well above 0.5 and the B-favoring class below 0.5, pushing the contrast toward positive values. Each class contains four unique pairs repeated 12 times, giving stable per-subject proportions.

This metric measures first-cue concordance: for each trial it finds the leftmost displayed feature on which options A and B differ, and codes 1 if the chosen option is the one favored by that feature. Display-order Take The Best predicts high concordance because the first displayed discriminator determines choice, with only weak validity-based modulation. Tallying predicts low concordance in this design: in the eight non-tied pairs the tally favors the opposite option, and in the four tally-balanced pairs it predicts 0.5. Averaging this code over all 96 trials produces a large mean separation and low per-subject variance, so the metric is stable with small human samples.

This metric isolates display-order directional responding on exactly the trials where Tallying has no preference. It selects tally-tie trials, where the feature-wise win counts for A and B are equal. For each first displayed discriminator position, it computes the average B choice rate when the B option is the first discriminator minus the average B choice rate when the A option is the first discriminator, then averages across those positions. Under Tallying, tally ties are uninformative and choice probability is 0.5 in both directions for every position, so this signed difference is close to 0. Under display-order Take The Best, the first discriminator controls choice: B-first trials produce mostly B responses and A-first trials produce mostly A responses. With the design validities 0.53, 0.91, 0.82 and the competing theory's beta/lambda ranges, the per-position differences are approximately 0.4 to 0.9, yielding a pooled value near 0.7. The within-subject signed contrast uses all 30 tally-tie trials per subject, keeping binomial estimation noise small, so the between-theory gap is large relative to between-subject variance.

For each trial, identify the first displayed feature that discriminates between the two options and code whether the response matched the side favored by that discriminating feature. Let c0 be the proportion of position-0 trials with such consistency, and c123 be the mean proportion for positions 1-3. The metric returns c123 - c0. Display-order TTB should produce a positive value because position 0 has low stated validity (0.55), making choices at that position less decisive than at high-validity positions 1-3 (0.85). The primacy-gradient accumulator should produce a negative value because its steep exponential position weights make position 0 dominate despite its lower validity, yielding the highest consistency at position 0 and declining consistency at later positions. This contrast uses both directions of each position and all trials, giving a large mean separation with small per-subject binomial noise.

This metric isolates trials where feature index 1 is the first discriminating feature. Feature 1 has stated validity 0.90, so the display-order TTB theory predicts that it should almost fully determine choice: when A has the high-validity cue, B-response rate is near 0.05; when B has it, B-response rate is near 0.95, producing a difference of roughly -0.90. The advocated capacity-sensitive accumulator has nearly flat weights for 12 features, so the same trials are decided by the accumulated tally. For the A-first index-1 trials the tally is negative or zero and for the B-first index-1 trials it is positive or zero, giving a B-rate difference near +0.59. The two theories therefore produce opposite signs and a large mean separation. Each category contains 24 trials per subject, so the metric also has low per-subject binomial variability.

This metric measures each subject's spread of A-choice frequencies across the eight unique trial types, then averages that within-subject variance. The eight unique trials form four mirror pairs, and every item is exactly balanced at 3 features versus 3 features. The advocated bounded-sampling accumulator has large subject-specific evidence-weight heterogeneity and a steep softmax/lapse transform, so for each mirror pair an individual subject tends to produce one near-impossible A-choice frequency and one near-certain frequency (with lapse, roughly 0.075 and 0.925). Across the eight trial-type frequencies this gives a large and stable within-subject variance (approximately 0.18 in expectation). In contrast, the competing capacity-sensitive accumulator has essentially fixed smooth primacy weights and a common beta, producing only moderate A-choice probabilities across the same eight trial types (approximately 0.23 to 0.77); its within-subject frequency variance is much smaller (approximately 0.04 including binomial noise). Because the metric is computed within subject and then averaged, it is insensitive to subject-level A/B response bias and should separate the two theories strongly with low between-subject variability.

The metric isolates the diagnostic trials in this design where the unweighted tally majority and the early high-validity block point in opposite directions. Every trial has a 4-3 tally margin, and the first three features have validity 0.95 while the last four have validity 0.55. The advocated theory predicts that the capacity collapse makes choices behave like an equal-weight tally, so subjects should choose the option favored by the unweighted tally on these conflict trials at roughly 0.94. The competing theory predicts validity-weighted sampling and a first-cue bonus, so on the same conflict trials subjects should often follow the early high-validity block instead, producing tally agreement around 0.43. The function identifies conflict rows automatically from the feature vectors, then returns the mean response agreement with the tally majority on those rows. Averaging 48 conflict trials per subject keeps the metric tightly estimated while preserving a large expected between-theory gap.
